arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found the refusal to reopen raised a new legal issue and was a new proceeding, thus jurisdiction existed.

arguments.claim: The Government submitted that the reopening of criminal proceedings was an extraordinary legal remedy and did not fall within the scope of Article 6 of the Convention.

anchor.surface_text: 59.�The Government argued that the application should be declared inadmissible as being incompatible ratione materiae with the provisions of the Convention, as the applicant’s complaints concerning the proceedings determining his application to have the criminal proceedings reopened did not fall within the scope of Article 6 of the Convention. In that connection, the Government firstly submitted that the reopening of criminal proceedings was an extraordinary legal remedy in Turkish criminal procedural law, as it was provided for in the third chapter of Book Six of the Code of Criminal Procedure entitled “Extraordinary legal remedies”.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court held Article 6 criminal limb applies where the domestic court determines the charge, which was the case here.

arguments.claim: The Government submitted that the trial court's examination of the reopening application was limited to admissibility and did not constitute a determination of a criminal charge, so Article 6 did not apply.

anchor.surface_text: 62.�The Government submitted that the trial court had first examined, under Article 319 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the admissibility of the applicant’s application to have the proceedings reopened, which had been based on the Court’s judgment in respect of him. Having found that the application had satisfied the criteria set out in that provision, the trial court had dismissed it under Article 321 § 1 of the same Code as being devoid of merit without holding a hearing, and the trial court had not been called upon to “determine a criminal charge”.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found the trial court's examination was likely determinative of the criminal charge and thus Article 6 applied.

arguments.claim: The applicant submitted that the domestic courts’ refusal of his application to have the criminal proceedings reopened had been arbitrary and unlawful, lacking sufficient examination and lawful basis, thus violating Article 6 § 1.

anchor.surface_text: 76.�The applicant submitted that the domestic courts’ refusal of his application to have the criminal proceedings reopened had been both arbitrary and unlawful, given that they had not made any enquiries in relation to his requests and statements and had not carried out a sufficient examination. Similarly, his application to the Constitutional Court had been dismissed as a result of an arbitrary attitude on the part of that court.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found the trial court's reasoning automatic and insufficient, failing to properly assess the applicant's submissions, violating Article 6 § 1.

arguments.claim: The Government submitted that the trial court had duly assessed the reopening application and dismissed it by a reasoned judgment stating grounds, including dismissal of witness requests based on the Court's prior findings.

anchor.surface_text: 77.�The Government submitted that the trial court had accepted, in line with Article 311 § 1 (f) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the applicant’s application for the reopening of the proceedings, which had been based on the Court’s finding of a violation, and had examined it in line with the Code. In doing so, the trial court had pursued the necessary correspondence to confirm whether the Court’s judgment had become final, had obtained the parties’ written observations on the application for reopening, and had examined the content of the previous proceedings resulting in his conviction, the Court’s judgment and the parties’ observations.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found the trial court's reasoning insufficient and automatic, failing to properly assess the applicant's submissions, thus rejecting the Government's claim.

arguments.claim: The Government submitted that the Court had not stated that reopening was necessarily the remedy for the violation found, only that it would be appropriate if requested by the applicant.

anchor.surface_text: 79.�In any event, the Government further submitted that in Davut Abo (cited above), the Court had not stated that the remedy for the violation found would necessarily be the reopening of criminal proceedings, but had only noted that it would be the most appropriate form of redress should the applicant so request.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found the trial court's dismissal without explanation contradicted the Court's prior judgment and was insufficient under Article 6 § 1.

arguments.claim: The trial court held that the procedural shortcoming could not be remedied by a retrial and had not affected the merits of the conviction, thus dismissing the reopening application.

anchor.surface_text: 83.�The Court observes that in dismissing the applicant’s application for the reopening of criminal proceedings, which was based on the Court’s finding of a violation of Article 6 §§ 1 and 3 (c) of the Convention in respect of him (see paragraph 13 above), the trial court relied on two grounds. It held firstly that the procedural shortcoming forming the basis of the Court’s judgment (i) could not be remedied by a retrial and secondly that (ii) it had not affected the merits of his final conviction.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found the reasoning automatic and insufficient, failing to properly assess the applicant's submissions, violating Article 6 § 1.

arguments.claim: The Court held that the trial court's view that the absence of a lawyer could not be remedied by a retrial was too unnuanced and excluded concrete assessment of the facts, falling short of Convention requirements.

anchor.surface_text: 84.�As regards the first ground, the Court reiterates that it has set out a non‑exhaustive list of factors which it has used in its case-law to assess the prejudice that the restrictions on the right to a lawyer may have had on the overall fairness of the proceedings (see, for a recapitulation of those criteria, Ibrahim and Others v. the United Kingdom [GC], nos. 50541/08 and 3 others, § 274, 13 September 2016).

arguments.claim: The Court held that the trial court's conclusion that the violation had not affected the merits of the conviction nullified the violation and contradicted the prior judgment's spirit.

anchor.surface_text: 87.�Regarding the second ground, the Court observes that, in the trial court’s view, so long as it was established that the applicant had not been subjected to ill-treatment while in police custody, the Court’s finding of a violation of Article 6 § 3 (c) of the Convention – due to the lack of legal assistance available to the applicant while in police custody – did not affect the merits of his final conviction.

arguments.claim: The Constitutional Court failed to address the shortcoming of the trial court's reasoning and dismissed the applicant's individual application, contrary to its own case-law.

anchor.surface_text: 89.�The Court notes that the Constitutional Court in its recent case-law on similar cases (see paragraphs 41 to 44) considered it more appropriate to exclude the evidence obtained in the absence of a lawyer. Taking into account the nature of the violation in the relevant case and the requirements arising from the Court’s findings, the Constitutional Court rejected arguments based on the sufficiency of the “remaining evidence” in the case file or on the claim that such violations could not be remedied through a retrial. However, in the present case, the Constitutional Court failed to address this shortcoming and dismissed the applicant’s individual application.

arguments.claim: The Government submitted that the length of the proceedings was reasonable and that judicial recess periods should be deducted from the calculation.

anchor.surface_text: 94.�The Government submitted that the proceedings in question had been conducted at three levels of jurisdiction, namely two different chambers of the Diyarbakır Fifth Assize Court and the Constitutional Court. In the Government’s view, even though the applicant had lodged his application for reopening on 7 April 2014, the length of the proceedings should be calculated from 18 February 2015.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court held the relevant period started from the lodging of the reopening application and that judicial recess should not be automatically deducted.

arguments.claim: The applicant complained that the length of the proceedings resulting in dismissal of his reopening application was excessive, violating Article 6 § 1.

There has therefore been a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention.

outcome.relief_summary: The Court found a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention concerning the unfairness of the proceedings related to the reopening application and the excessive length of those proceedings. The Court dismissed the Government's preliminary objections and held that the criminal limb of Article 6 was applicable. It concluded that the trial court's dismissal of the reopening application was based on automatic and insufficient reasoning and that the Constitutional Court failed to remedy that shortcoming, thus violating Article 6 § 1. The Court also found the length of the proceedings excessive and incompatible with the reasonable time requirement under Article 6 § 1.
directions: The trial court must conduct a fresh and thorough examination of the reopening application in compliance with Article 6 guarantees.
Domestic courts must show due diligence in assessing reopening requests based on the Court's findings to ensure practical and effective execution of judgments.
The Constitutional Court should align its assessments with the requirements of Article 6 and the Court's case-law to avoid arbitrariness.
